title: Mushroom Bodies
intro: Mushroom bodies are paired neuropils in the insect brain, named for their stalk-and-cap shape, that sit at the center of olfactory learning. A fly or a bee smells thousands of odors through a few dozen (fly) to about 160 (bee) kinds of receptor. The mushroom body turns those overlapping inputs into sparse, distinct patterns and then learns which patterns mean food and which mean danger. It is one of the best-understood learning circuits in any brain, and a compact model of ideas that also matter for cortex: expansion, sparseness, and learning only at the readout.

items: Projection neurons (PNs). In the fruit fly about 50 types of olfactory glomeruli in the antennal lobe each send projection neurons to the mushroom body calyx (and to the lateral horn, which handles innate responses). An odor activates a dense, overlapping subset of them. Similar odors give similar PN patterns.

Kenyon cells (KCs). About 2000 Kenyon cells per mushroom body in Drosophila, and many tens of thousands or more in insects such as bees and cockroaches. Each KC receives input from only a handful of PNs through claw-shaped dendrites: about 7 claws on average in the fly (range 2-11), wired to an apparently random set of glomeruli (Caron et al. 2013). Counts from electron-microscopy connectomes come out a little lower, about 5-6. That few-onto-many expansion is the core trick.

Global inhibition. A single large GABAergic neuron in the fly (APL) gets input from all KCs and inhibits them all. Together with KCs' high firing thresholds, it keeps only about 5-10% of KCs active for any odor (Turner, Bazhenov & Laurent 2008; Lin et al. 2014).

Output neurons (MBONs). The KC axons run in parallel through the lobes and converge onto about 34 mushroom body output neurons in the fly, organized into compartments (Aso et al. 2014). Each MBON's activity biases behavior toward approach or avoidance.

Dopaminergic neurons (DANs). Each compartment also receives dopaminergic input that signals reward or punishment. When a DAN fires while a KC is active, the KC-to-MBON synapse in that compartment changes: in the fly, mostly depression. This is a three-factor learning rule, like reward-modulated STDP.

blocks.text: Learning happens only at the KC-to-MBON synapses. The expansion layer is fixed and random. Because KC codes are sparse and nearly non-overlapping, a reward-driven change for one odor barely affects the response to another.

The widget builds a model mushroom body: 50 PNs, 2000 KCs, each KC summing a random set of PNs, and a threshold set so that a chosen percentage of KCs fire, standing in for APL inhibition. It then morphs a base odor into others by swapping active PNs and plots how much the KC codes overlap (y) against how much the PN codes overlap (x). Points below the diagonal mean the mushroom body has made similar odors more different.

widget.title: Kenyon-cell code overlap against PN code overlap

config.xLabel: PN code overlap between two odors

items: At the defaults (6 inputs, within the fly's measured range, 5% active), odors with 60% PN overlap share only about a quarter of their KCs. The curve hugs zero for dissimilar odors and rises steeply only near identity.
Raise the active fraction to 20-50%. The curve moves toward the diagonal: a denser code separates less. Sparseness, enforced by inhibition, is what decorrelates.

Set inputs per KC to 1-2. Each KC just copies one or two PNs, so the code inherits the PNs' overlap. With very many inputs, every KC sees nearly the same average and the code loses detail. Litwin-Kumar et al. (2017) showed that a handful of inputs per cell, close to what the fly has, maximizes the dimensionality of the KC representation.

blocks.text: A hashing algorithm, and a decision maker

Dasgupta, Stevens and Navlakha (2017) pointed out that this circuit implements a locality-sensitive hash: a sparse random expansion followed by winner-take-all keeps similar odors similar and dissimilar ones far apart, and it beat standard hashing methods at similarity search. It is an example of a biological circuit becoming a computer-science algorithm.

The output side is more than a lookup table. MBONs carry valence (approach or avoid), and compartments interact, so the mushroom body can combine learned value with context. In freely walking cockroaches, Mizunami and colleagues (1998) recorded mushroom body extrinsic (output) neurons of three kinds: some told self-generated from imposed sensory stimulation, some tracked the animal's own movements, and some began firing before episodes of locomotion and changed their activity with the turning direction. That suggests the output carries something closer to a motor decision than a label, but it rests on a small number of recordings: treat it as a suggestive finding, not settled consensus.

The mushroom body shares its design with the cerebellum (mossy fibers onto many granule cells, read out by Purkinje cells) and arguably with the cortical input layer: expand into a high-dimensional, sparse code with fixed or slowly learned weights, then learn fast at a linear readout.

For a cortical column: copy three things. First, a sparse expansion with strong global inhibition (a winner-take-all layer, see #/snn/encoding and the winner-take-all widget at #/neuroscience/cortical-columns/column-blueprint) gives you distinct codes for similar inputs, as HTM's spatial pooler intends. Second, learning at the readout with a three-factor rule (#/snn/learning-rules/stdp-reward) attaches value without disturbing the code. Third, it is a small, fully mapped circuit: a good first target to build and verify in SNN form before attempting a column.
